title: The Words Between: How Journalists Report What People Say
paragraphs: Read any newspaper article and you will notice that very little of it consists of direct quotation. Journalists rarely reproduce entire speeches or interviews verbatim. Instead, they select, paraphrase, and frame what was said — and the tools they use for this are the reporting verbs of English. These verbs are not neutral. Every choice a journalist makes about how to introduce reported speech carries information about how they want the reader to interpret what was said.

Consider a simple statement from a university rector: "The institution will expand its research funding next year." A journalist could report this in at least five distinct ways. They could write that the rector said the institution would expand its research funding. This is neutral — it presents the information without evaluation. But they could also write that the rector claimed the institution would expand, implying that this is something that might not actually happen, or might be disputed. They could write that the rector promised, which creates a commitment that can later be held against him if the funding does not materialise. They could write that the rector announced, suggesting a formal and deliberate statement. Or they could write that the rector suggested, making the statement sound tentative rather than definite.

Each of these choices — said, claimed, promised, announced, suggested — conveys a different relationship between the speaker and their words. Claimed implies doubt or opposition. Promised implies commitment. Admitted implies that the speaker was reluctant or that the information is somewhat uncomfortable. Insisted implies that the speaker had to push back against resistance. Warned implies a threat or serious concern. These implications exist even when the original words were identical.

This is why academic and professional readers have learned to read reporting verbs carefully. When a politician's spokesperson is described as having "confirmed" something, it carries more weight than if they merely "noted" it. When an expert "warned" that something might happen, the reader should understand that the journalist is presenting this as more alarming than if the expert had simply "said" it. The verb is doing editorial work.

The implications of reporting verbs also cross languages and cultures, which creates interesting challenges for translators and journalists working across linguistic contexts. The Kazakh language, like Russian, has its own range of verbs for introducing reported speech, and they do not map cleanly onto English equivalents. The verb that in Kazakh implies mild reservation might become "claimed" in English, which implies stronger doubt. The translator must make a choice, and that choice changes the text.

Understanding reported speech is not only a grammatical skill. It is a critical literacy skill — the ability to read a text carefully enough to notice not just what the words say but how they are framed. A politician who "denied the allegations" is in a different position from one who "rejected the claims." A company that "admitted fault" is in a different position from one that "acknowledged shortcomings." The differences are legal, ethical, and political. And they are expressed through the grammar of reported speech.

For students of English at B1 level and above, the goal is not simply to be able to convert direct speech to indirect speech and apply the correct tense shifts. The goal is to understand and use reported speech as a tool for precise, nuanced communication — to be able to write "she insisted that the deadline would not be moved" and understand that this tells the reader something very specific about the speaker's position, far beyond simply reporting what she said.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I noticed the journalist used "claimed" when reporting what the minister said. That already tells you something.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Right — "claimed" implies doubt. If they'd written "said," it would just be neutral information.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: And "admitted" implies something uncomfortable. Like the person didn't want to say it but had to.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I never thought about it that way. I just read "he said" or "she said" and moved on.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's exactly what editors count on. If you don't notice the verbs, you don't notice the framing.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: So reading carefully means reading the reporting verbs as carefully as the content.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Yes. The verb is doing editorial work. It's not just grammar — it's a position.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: That changes how I'll read the news from now on.

keyPhrases.context: "Journalists rarely reproduce speeches verbatim." = word for word, exactly as spoken.
"They paraphrase what was said." = restate in different words.
"They frame what was said." = present it in a particular way to suggest an interpretation.
"'Claimed' implies doubt." = suggests something without directly stating it.
"If the funding doesn't materialise." = if it doesn't actually happen.
"The verb is doing editorial work." = making a judgement, not just reporting.
"Nuanced communication." = with subtle distinctions and careful shades of meaning.
"Making the statement sound tentative." = uncertain, not definite.

vocab.definition: in exactly the same words as were used originally
vocab.example: Journalists rarely quote politicians verbatim — they select and paraphrase.

vocab.definition: to suggest something without directly stating it
vocab.example: "Claimed" implies doubt about whether the statement is true.

vocab.definition: not certain or definite; done cautiously as a trial
vocab.example: "Suggested" makes a statement sound tentative rather than definite.

vocab.definition: not supporting any side; not expressing a view
vocab.example: "Said" is the most neutral reporting verb — it doesn't imply evaluation.
"Admitted" implies the speaker was reluctant to share the information.

vocab.definition: a claim that someone has done something wrong, without proof
vocab.example: A politician who "denied the allegations" vs one who "rejected the claims."

vocab.definition: relating to moral principles; morally correct
vocab.example: The differences between reporting verbs have legal, ethical, and political weight.

vocab.definition: a failure to meet a required standard; a weakness
vocab.example: A company that "acknowledged shortcomings" vs one that "admitted fault."

"The rector said the institution WOULD expand." — "would" instead of "will" because:
opts: Tense backshift: will→would in reported speech
questions.correct: Tense backshift: will→would in reported speech
